name: רציפה_ללא_נגזרות_חלקיות
questiontext:
In this exercise and the few that follow it, we will discuss continuity, partial derivatives and differentiability of functions that are not elementary at the origin. Take for example the function

Let \( f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}{{CT:0}} & (x,y)\neq (0,0) \\0 & (x,y)=(0,0)\end{array}\right. \).

Here is the graph of this function. It was created by typing "x*sin(20/(x+y))" at a google bar. Before going on, please take a few minutes and try it out yourself!

First, calcuate the partial derivatives of \(f(x,y)\) when \((x,y)\neq (0,0)\). 

Remark: The answer will be Printed as the program interprets it, please verify it's as expected.

 

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((x,y)\)=[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((x,y)\)=[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

 

Is \(f(x,y)\) continuous on \(R^2\)? [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]

 

Now calculate the partial derivatives at zero. If they do not exist, please enter "false"

 

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((0,0)\)=[[input:ans5]] [[validation:ans5]]

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((0,0)\)=[[input:ans6]] [[validation:ans6]]

 

Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives?[[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]]

on_true.feedback: Continuity at zero: Correct answer, \(f(x,y)\) is indeed continuous. For all \((x,y)\neq(0,0) \), \(f(x,y)\) is an elementary function, therefore continuous. And for \((x,y)=(0,0) \) \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}x \cdot sin(\frac{1}{x+y})=0=f(0,0) \), therefore also continuous at \((0,0)\).

on_false.feedback: Continuity at zero: Inorrect answer, \(f(x,y)\) is continuous. It is definitely continuous at any \((x,y) \ne (0,0)\). And it turns out that it is continuous at the origin too. Try calculating the limit and find out for yourself. You can use the fact that \(\left| sin(1/(x+y)) \right| < 1\).

on_true.feedback: Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives: Your answer is correct. Our function here \(f(x,y)=\){{CT:1}} is an example. For \((x,y)=(0,0) f\) is continuous, but \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0} sin(\frac{20}{h}) \), therefore \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)\) doen't exist.

on_false.feedback: Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives: Your answer is incorrect. In fact our function here is a counterexample. If you answer all the other questions correctly you will see that this is a continuous function that does not admit a well defined partial derivative in the \(x\) direction.

on_true.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) \): Indeed this partial derivative is not defined. When we try to evaluate it we substitute \(y=0\) and differentiating with respect to \(x\). Thus obtaining the derivative \(= \frac{d}{dx} x sin(\frac{20}{x})\). And (hopefully) we remember from calculus one that this derivative does not exist.

on_false.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) \): Please try again. Remember to evaluate \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) \) we have to substitute \(y=0\) and differentiate the resulting function of \(x\) with respect to \(x\).

on_true.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \): Your answer is correct. To evaluate \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \) we have to substitute \(x=0\) and then differentiate the resulting function. What we get, is the easiest function to differentiate. \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) = \frac{d}{dy} 0_{y=0} = 0 \). Note that we found a function that has one partial derivative but not the other. Do go back to the graph of the function now and see if you understand how this happens!

on_false.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \): Please try again. Remember to evaluate \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \) we have to substitute \(x=0\) and differentiate the resulting function of \(y\) with respect to \(y\).
